ch01.title: The Flood
ch01.summary: Why nearly every people who kept records remembers the world ending in water — the Mesopotamian lineage from Ziusudra to Utnapishtim, its relationship to Genesis, and what the archaeology will and won't support.
ch01.plateCaption: The vessel upon the rising waters — the shared image of the flood myths compared in this chapter. An original illustration of the motif, not any one tradition’s telling.

ch46.title: Creation & the First Order
ch46.summary: How the world began, told side by side: the watery chaos of Tiamat, Nun, and tehom; the combat myth (chaoskampf) in which Marduk, Baal, and Zeus win order by battle — and Genesis's pointed refusal of the fight; the world built from a slain primordial body (Ymir, Purusha) and the contested Indo-European 'cosmic giant'; creation by word from Ptah to 'let there be'; the later doctrine of creation from nothing and the Genesis 1:1 translation debate; and the astonishing Nasadiya Sukta, the ancient hymn that looks at the beginning and admits it cannot be sure. With a symbology of the cosmic egg, sacred number, the dividing line, and the creative word.

ch46.plateCaption: The first light above, the dividing of the waters, and the first mound rising from the deep. An original schematic of the creation motif, not a historical illustration.

ch47.title: Journeys to the Underworld
ch47.summary: The descent to the land of the dead — one of the oldest and most widespread of all sacred stories — and what a civilization reveals when it weighs its dead. Inanna stripped at the seven gates; the Greek katabasis (Odysseus, Orpheus, Aeneas, Persephone); Egypt’s Duat and the Weighing of the Heart against the feather of Maat; the judged afterlives (Zoroastrian Chinvat bridge, the Tibetan bardo, Chinese Diyu) set against the un-judged pits of Sheol and Norse Hel; the god who goes down (Izanagi, Baldr, the Harrowing of Hell); and a symbology of the gate, the ferryman, the scale, and the guidebook written for the dead.
ch47.plateCaption: A gate at the top of a stair leading down, and below it the river with a ferryman’s boat: the threshold, the descent and the crossing that recur in the underworld journeys of many traditions. An original composite, not a copy of any single tradition’s image.

ch48.title: The Great Goddess
ch48.summary: The divine feminine — and the modern myth built on top of it. The goddesses we can actually document (Inanna/Ishtar, Isis, Asherah and the ‘Yahweh and his Asherah’ inscriptions, Cybele, Demeter, the living Mahādevī of India, Guanyin, Amaterasu); the ancient temptation to unify them into one; and Marija Gimbutas’s Great Goddess of a peaceful Neolithic matriarchy, reported honestly as largely rejected by mainstream archaeology. The sublimation of the goddess into Wisdom/Sophia and the Virgin Mary; the 20th-century Goddess movement and thealogy; and a symbology of the figurine, the triple moon, and the Black Madonna — a study in keeping what is revered separate from what is proven.

ch48.plateCaption: The waxing, full and waning moon, the “triple form” linked with some goddesses, above a schematic seated figurine. An interpretive drawing, not a copy of any particular figurine; what prehistoric figurines meant is unknown.

ch49.title: Sacred Kingship
ch49.summary: The ruler as a holy figure between heaven and earth — god, god’s son, god’s chosen, or god’s hostage. Frazer’s priest of Nemi and the dying-king thesis; the king as god (the Egyptian pharaoh, the Sapa Inca son of the Sun, the Japanese emperor, the deified Roman emperor); the king answerable to Heaven (the Chinese Mandate of Heaven, the prophet-checked king of Israel); the documented dying-king rites (the Shilluk reth, the Mesopotamian substitute king); and anointed kingship in Christendom (divine right, the royal touch, messiah/Christ). A symbology of regalia, anointing oil, and the king’s two bodies — with Frazer’s grand unifying thesis flagged honestly as rejected even where the specific cases hold.
ch49.plate: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" class="plate-art" viewBox="0 0 200 200" fill="none" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M58 88 L66 50 L83 72 L100 40 L117 72 L134 50 L142 88 Z" stroke="#e7c680" stroke-width="1.6"/><line x1="58" y1="96" x2="142" y2="96" stroke="#e7c680" stroke-width="1.6"/><g fill="#e7c680"><circle cx="66" cy="48" r="3"/><circle cx="100" cy="37" r="3.4"/><circle cx="134" cy="48" r="3"/><circle cx="100" cy="80" r="3"/></g><path d="M70 150 C80 118 112 110 136 118 L132 128 C114 124 92 132 84 154 Z" stroke="#e7c680" stroke-width="1.4"/><g fill="#e7c680" opacity="0.8"><circle cx="76" cy="162" r="2"/><circle cx="73" cy="172" r="1.8"/><circle cx="75" cy="182" r="1.5"/></g></svg>
ch49.plateCaption: A crown above a horn of anointing oil: the two great signs of sacred kingship, the ruler crowned and the ruler anointed. An interpretive composite, not any particular regalia.

ch50.title: The End of Days
ch50.summary: How the world ends — and the deep divide between the line and the wheel. The Qumran War Scroll and the apocalyptic mind; the Persian blueprint (Zoroastrian dualism, the Saoshyant, resurrection, and Frashokereti, the ‘making wonderful’); the apocalyptic turn in Second Temple Judaism (Daniel, Enoch) and the contested question of Zoroastrian influence; the Book of Revelation, the Antichrist, and the millennium; the Islamic Day of Resurrection, the Mahdi, and the Dajjal; and the cyclical counter-vision — Norse Ragnarök, the Hindu Kali Yuga and Kalki, Buddhist Maitreya, the Aztec Fifth Sun — where destruction is one turn of an eternal wheel. A symbology of 666, Armageddon, and the world made new.
ch50.plateCaption: Above, history as a line with seven stations, running to a final burst of light; below, time as a wheel that turns without end. The two visions of the end compared in the chapter, drawn as an original diagram.

ch51.title: Sacrifice & the Scapegoat
ch51.summary: The gift of blood — one of the most universal and most troubling of religious acts. What sacrifice was (korban, ‘drawing near’; yajna into fire; thysia, ‘making smoke’; do ut des) and the gift/communion/feeding theories; blood on the altar; the substitution of animal for human (the Aqedah, the Passover lamb); human sacrifice reported honestly (Aztec, the contested Carthaginian tophet, Shang retainers); the scapegoat of Leviticus and the Greek pharmakos; Girard’s mimetic scapegoat mechanism and Burkert’s Homo Necans (flagged as contested); and the sacrifice that ends sacrifice — the Lamb of God and the Eucharist, the bloodless turns of Judaism, Hinduism, Jainism, and Buddhism. A symbology of altar, smoke, substitute, and shared meal.

ch51.plateCaption: A horned altar with smoke rising, and a scarlet thread: the gift that goes up to the gods, and the Day of Atonement rite of Leviticus 16. An original rendering, not a specific altar.

v32.title: The Popol Vuh Manuscript
v32.dated: Copied c. 1700–1715 by Francisco Ximénez; the lost K'iche' original c. 1550s
v32.summary: The K'iche' Maya book of creation, the Hero Twins and the lords of Xibalba, which survives only because a Dominican friar in Chichicastenango copied it around 1701, K'iche' beside Spanish. The alphabetic original, written by K'iche' nobles after the conquest, is lost.

v31.title: The Dresden Codex
v31.dated: Usually dated 11th–14th century; the date is debated
v31.held: SLUB Dresden (Saxon State and University Library), Mscr.Dresd.R.310
v31.summary: The finest of the four Maya books that survived the Spanish conquest: a folding screen of bark paper, bought in Vienna in 1739 and damaged by water in 1945. Its tables track Venus, predict eclipse seasons, and bind both to the sacred 260-day count.

v41.title: The Codex Borgia
v41.dated: Late 15th or early 16th century, central Mexico
v41.summary: A painted screenfold of deerskin from the Puebla–Tlaxcala region of Mexico, among the very few divinatory books to survive the conquest. It is a manual of the 260-day count, with gods, omens, a Venus almanac and a mysterious central section that may describe a journey through the night.

v45.title: The Nebra Sky Disc
v45.dated: Buried c. 1600 BCE (Early Bronze Age); a later date was proposed in 2020 and rejected by most specialists
v45.held: State Museum of Prehistory, Halle (Saale), Germany
v45.summary: A bronze disc 30 cm across with a gold sun or full moon, a crescent and 32 stars, among them a cluster read as the Pleiades. It was dug up by looters in 1999, recovered in a Swiss police sting in 2002, and altered at least four times in antiquity. It may be the oldest known concrete depiction of the sky.

v61.title: The Kojiki: the Shinpukuji Manuscript
v61.dated: Text completed 712 CE; oldest manuscript copied 1371–1372
v61.summary: The 'Record of Ancient Matters', presented to the Japanese court in 712: the birth of the gods, Izanagi and Izanami, the sun goddess Amaterasu, and the descent of the emperors. Its oldest surviving copy was made by a monk of Shinpukuji in 1371–72 and is a National Treasure of Japan.

v69.title: The Kumulipo
v69.dated: Composed in the 18th century for the chief Kalaninuiamamao; first printed 1889
v69.held: Printed for King Kalākaua in 1889; Queen Liliʻuokalani's English translation published in 1897
v69.summary: A Hawaiian creation chant of 2,102 lines in sixteen ages, from the first night and the birth of the coral polyp to the gods and the chiefs. Composed in honour of an 18th-century chief, printed by King Kalākaua in 1889, and translated by the deposed Queen Liliʻuokalani while she was held prisoner.

v20.title: The Papyrus of Ani
v20.summary: A 24-metre Book of the Dead made for the scribe Ani at Thebes. Its judgment scene, the heart weighed against the feather of Ma'at before the Devourer, is the most famous image of the afterlife from the ancient world. Spell 125 and the 42 denials of the Negative Confession.

v34.title: The Pyramid Texts of Unas
v34.dated: Carved c. 2350 BCE (end of the 5th Dynasty)
v34.held: In place: the Pyramid of Unas, Saqqara, Egypt
v34.summary: The oldest large body of religious writing in the world: 283 spells carved and painted blue on the walls of a king's burial chambers under a ceiling of stars. They were meant for no living reader, and were found in 1881. They include the notorious 'Cannibal Hymn'.

v37.title: The Gundestrup Cauldron
v37.dated: Made c. 150 BCE–1st century CE; found 1891
v37.summary: Nine kilograms of gilded silver, taken apart and laid in a Danish bog. Its plates show an antlered figure holding a torc and a serpent, a giant dipping a man into a vat, and a bull sacrifice. Probably made far to the south-east. Celtic gods, Thracian silversmiths, or both?

v39.title: The Derveni Papyrus
v39.dated: Roll c. 340–320 BCE; the text composed c. 400 BCE
v39.summary: A papyrus roll half-burned on a funeral pyre near Thessaloniki, the oldest surviving book in Europe. It is a philosopher's allegorical commentary on a secret Orphic poem about the birth of the gods, which opens by telling the uninitiated to shut the doors.

v13.title: The Tilma of Guadalupe
v13.dated: Devotion attested by 1556; tradition dates the image to 1531
v13.held: Basilica of Our Lady of Guadalupe, Mexico City
v13.summary: The cloak venerated as Juan Diego's, bearing the image of Our Lady of Guadalupe. It was attacked in 1556 as 'painted by an Indian, Marcos', survived a bomb in 1921, and was studied in infrared in 1979. The Nahuatl account, the documents, the science and the myths, kept apart.

v59.title: The Venus of Willendorf
v59.summary: An 11-centimetre limestone figure of a woman with no face, found beside the Danube in 1908. She is perhaps the most famous image of the Ice Age. The name 'Venus' is a modern joke, and her meaning is unknown. A 2022 scan traced her stone to northern Italy.

v14.title: The Holy Grail
v14.held: Claimants in Valencia, Genoa, León and elsewhere
v14.summary: The Gospels mention a cup and say nothing of its fate. The Grail was born in French romance around 1190. Valencia's agate cup, Genoa's glass dish and León's onyx chalice, set against the literature that made them sacred, and the modern 'bloodline' hoax.

v05.title: The Holy Lance (“Spear of Destiny”)
v05.held: Vienna (Imperial Treasury), Rome (St Peter's), Etchmiadzin (Armenia); copy in Kraków
v05.summary: One Gospel sentence, four rival spearheads, and a 1970s occult myth. The Habsburg lance's gold sleeve reads LANCEA ET CLAVVS DOMINI, but metallurgy dates the blade centuries after the Crucifixion, and the 'Spear of Destiny' Hitler legend traces to a single 1972 book.

v06.title: The Crown of Thorns
v06.dated: Documented from 1238 (Paris); earlier history by tradition; never dated
v06.held: Notre-Dame de Paris (axial chapel, reliquary of 2024)
v06.summary: A ring of bundled rushes bound with gold thread, with no thorns left on it, for which Saint Louis paid almost half his annual revenue and built the Sainte-Chapelle. Traced from the Gospel mockery through Constantinople, Venice and the Revolution to the night Notre-Dame burned.

v23.title: The Tel Dan Stele
v23.summary: Three basalt fragments of an Aramaean king's boast, dug up in 1993–94, naming a king of Israel and bytdwd, the 'House of David'. The first mention of David outside the Bible, what it proves and what it doesn't.

v27.title: The Sacred Tooth Relic
v27.dated: In Sri Lanka since the 4th century CE (tradition)
v27.held: Sri Dalada Maligawa (Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic), Kandy
v27.summary: The Buddha's tooth, smuggled to Sri Lanka in a princess's hair according to the chronicle, carried in procession by elephants each year. For a thousand years it was the proof of a king's right to rule. The Portuguese claimed to have burned it in 1561.

v35.title: The Cyrus Cylinder
v35.summary: A clay barrel inscribed in Babylonian cuneiform after Cyrus of Persia took Babylon. It praises Cyrus as Marduk's chosen king and records the return of gods and peoples to their homes. It is often called the first charter of human rights, which it is not, and it is read beside the Bible's decree of Cyrus.

v43.title: The Merneptah Stele
v43.summary: A pharaoh's granite hymn of victory, found by Flinders Petrie in 1896. Of its 28 lines, one names Israel, about 3,200 years ago, the earliest certain mention of Israel anywhere. The hieroglyphs say something precise about what Israel was.

v46.title: The Piprahwa Relics
v46.dated: Stupa deposit c. 3rd–2nd century BCE or earlier (debated)
v46.held: Indian Museum, Kolkata; National Museum, New Delhi; gems returned to India in 2025
v46.summary: Bone fragments, a soapstone urn and some 1,800 gems dug from a stupa in 1898 by a British estate manager. The urn's inscription says the shrine holds relics of the Buddha, or of the Buddha's kinsmen, depending on how it is read. In 2025 India halted a Sotheby's sale of the gems.

v53.title: The Rosetta Stone
v53.summary: A priestly decree honouring the boy-king Ptolemy V, carved in hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek. Found by French soldiers in 1799, taken by the British in 1801, and used by Thomas Young and Jean-François Champollion to crack the Egyptian script. Egypt asks for its return.

v54.title: The Behistun Inscription
v54.held: In place: Mount Bisotun, Kermanshah Province, Iran (UNESCO World Heritage Site)
v54.summary: Darius the Great's account of how he seized the Persian throne, carved about 60 metres up a cliff in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian, beneath a relief of the king and the winged symbol of Ahuramazda. Copied at great risk by Henry Rawlinson, it opened cuneiform to modern reading.

v55.title: The Oracle Bones of Anyang
v55.held: Institute of History and Philology, Academia Sinica (Taipei); Institute of Archaeology and museums in China; collections worldwide
v55.summary: Turtle shells and cattle shoulder-blades that Shang kings had cracked in fire to put questions to their ancestors, then had the questions and answers carved beside the cracks. Sold as 'dragon bones' for medicine until 1899, they are the oldest body of Chinese writing.

v66.title: The Kebra Nagast
v66.dated: Compiled c. 1314–1322 CE; surviving manuscripts mostly later
v66.held: Many Ge'ez manuscripts in Ethiopia and in European libraries (British Library's Magdala collection among them)
v66.summary: Ethiopia's 'Glory of the Kings': how the Queen of Sheba visited Solomon, bore his son Menelik, and how Menelik brought the Ark of the Covenant to Aksum. It gave the Solomonic dynasty its legitimacy for 650 years, and it is revered by Rastafari. A copy looted from Magdala was returned to Ethiopia in 1872.

v02.title: The Dead Sea Scrolls
v02.held: Israel Antiquities Authority & The Israel Museum, Jerusalem
v02.summary: Some 900–1,000 manuscripts from eleven caves near Qumran — the oldest copies of the Hebrew Bible, lost scriptures like Enoch and Jubilees, a sect's rules and war-liturgy, cryptic alphabets, a treasure list on copper — and the forgeries that followed them onto the market.

v36.title: The Rök Runestone
v36.summary: A granite slab carrying the longest runic inscription in the world, some 760 runes, raised by a father for his dead son. It is full of riddles and written partly in cipher, and it names Theodoric the Great. No two scholars read it quite the same way.

v49.title: The Book of Enoch
v49.dated: Written 3rd century BCE–1st century CE; Qumran fragments c. 200 BCE onwards; Ge'ez manuscripts from the 14th–15th century
v49.held: Complete text in Ge'ez manuscripts (Ethiopia and European libraries); Aramaic fragments from Qumran (Israel Antiquities Authority)
v49.summary: The book of the Watchers, the fallen angels who taught forbidden arts, and of Enoch's journeys through the heavens. Quoted in the New Testament's Letter of Jude, dropped by most churches, and preserved whole only in Ethiopia, where it is Scripture.

noah.name: Noah
noah.desc: Saved with his family and the animals from the flood in Genesis 6–9; God's covenant with him is sealed by the rainbow. Nūḥ is a prophet in the Qur'an.
noah.contested: The story has close parallels in older Mesopotamian flood stories; see The Flood (ch01).

enki.name: Enki / Ea
enki.desc: God of fresh water, wisdom and crafts, who warns the flood hero to build a boat.

gilgamesh.name: Gilgamesh
gilgamesh.desc: Hero of the Epic of Gilgamesh, who seeks immortality after the death of his friend Enkidu and hears the story of the flood from Utnapishtim.
gilgamesh.contested: A king of this name may have ruled Uruk around 2700 BCE. It is not proven.

adam.name: Adam
adam.desc: Formed from the dust of the ground and placed in the garden of Eden (Genesis 2), then sent out to till the soil. In the Qur'an, Ādam is the first prophet.

eve.name: Eve
eve.desc: The first woman, who eats the forbidden fruit at the serpent's urging (Genesis 3). Genesis does not name the fruit; the apple comes from later Latin tradition.

marduk.name: Marduk
marduk.desc: Patron god of Babylon. In the Enuma Elish he defeats Tiamat, builds the world from her body and is made king of the gods.

tiamat.name: Tiamat
tiamat.desc: Primordial goddess of the salt waters in the Enuma Elish, mother of the first gods, split in two by Marduk to make heaven and earth.
tiamat.contested: Modern images of Tiamat as a dragon are interpretation. The Enuma Elish never clearly describes her form.

kumarbi.name: Kumarbi
kumarbi.desc: In the Hurrian Kumarbi cycle he seizes the kingship of heaven from Anu, a succession myth often compared with Hesiod's story of Kronos.

gaia.name: Gaia
gaia.desc: In Hesiod's Theogony, Earth, who emerges after Chaos and gives birth to Ouranos, the sky.

brahma.name: Brahma
brahma.desc: Four-faced creator god, born from a lotus rising from Vishnu's navel in later myth. He has very few temples of his own.

izanagi.name: Izanagi
izanagi.desc: With Izanami, stirs the ocean with a jewelled spear to make the islands of Japan. Returning from the land of the dead, he washes and gives birth to the sun, moon and storm.

izanami.name: Izanami
izanami.desc: Co-creator of the islands and gods of Japan, who dies giving birth to fire and becomes the ruler of Yomi, the land of the dead.

maize-god.name: The Maize God
maize-god.desc: Young god whose death and rebirth follow the cycle of the maize; on Classic Maya vessels he rises from the split earth.

viracocha.name: Viracocha
viracocha.desc: Creator god who, in myths written down after the Spanish conquest, rises from Lake Titicaca, makes the sun and moon and walks away across the sea.
viracocha.contested: He is often identified with the Staff God of Tiwanaku, which is centuries older than the Inca. That identification is not proven.

tangaroa.name: Tangaroa
tangaroa.desc: Great god of the ocean across Polynesia (Tangaloa in Samoa, Kanaloa in Hawaii), in some islands the creator.

sky-woman.name: Sky Woman
sky-woman.epithet: She who fell from the sky
sky-woman.desc: In Haudenosaunee creation, the woman who falls from the sky world and lands on the back of a turtle, where the earth is made.

osiris.name: Osiris
osiris.desc: Murdered by his brother Set and restored by the magic of Isis, Osiris became king of the underworld and the model for every Egyptian's hope of new life.

anubis.name: Anubis
anubis.desc: Jackal-headed god of embalming and cemeteries, who guides the dead and oversees the weighing of the heart in the Book of the Dead.

inanna.name: Inanna / Ishtar
inanna.desc: Sumerian goddess of love, sex and war, called Ishtar in Akkadian and linked with the planet Venus. Her descent to the underworld is among the oldest surviving myths.

ereshkigal.name: Ereshkigal
ereshkigal.desc: Ruler of the underworld and sister of Inanna, who has her sister struck dead when she descends into her realm.

hades.name: Hades
hades.desc: Ruler of the underworld and brother of Zeus, who carried off Persephone. Greeks often avoided his name and called him Plouton, 'the wealthy one'.

persephone.name: Persephone
persephone.desc: Daughter of Demeter, taken by Hades. Her return each year from the underworld was at the heart of the Eleusinian Mysteries.

orpheus.name: Orpheus
orpheus.desc: Legendary poet whose music moved beasts and stones, who went down to the underworld for his wife Eurydice. Poems in his name were the scripture of the Orphics.

hel.name: Hel
hel.desc: Daughter of Loki, ruler of the realm of those who die of sickness or old age, described by Snorri as half dark and half flesh-coloured.

baldr.name: Baldr
baldr.desc: Son of Odin and Frigg, loved by all, killed through Loki's trickery by a dart of mistletoe; he returns after Ragnarök.

hero-twins.name: The Hero Twins
hero-twins.desc: Twins of the Popol Vuh, who defeat the lords of the underworld, Xibalba, in a ball game and rise as the sun and the moon.

baron-samedi.name: Baron Samedi
baron-samedi.desc: Head of the Gede, the lwa of death and the dead in Haitian Vodou, dressed in top hat and tails, bawdy, and also a healer.

lazarus.name: Lazarus
lazarus.desc: Brother of Martha and Mary of Bethany, whom Jesus raises from the tomb after four days (John 11).

hathor.name: Hathor
hathor.desc: Goddess of love, music, joy and the sky, shown as a cow or as a woman wearing cow horns and a sun disk.

asherah.name: Asherah
asherah.desc: Mother goddess of Ugarit and consort of El, whose symbol was a sacred tree or wooden pole.
asherah.contested: Inscriptions from Kuntillet Ajrud mention 'Yahweh and his Asherah'. Whether she was once worshipped as Yahweh's consort is debated.

anahita.name: Anahita
anahita.desc: Goddess of the waters, fertility and healing, praised in the Avesta and honoured with temples under the Achaemenid and Sasanian kings.

demeter.name: Demeter
demeter.desc: Goddess of grain and harvest, whose search for her lost daughter was the founding myth of the Mysteries at Eleusis.

artemis.name: Artemis
artemis.desc: Twin sister of Apollo, virgin huntress, protector of wild animals and of women in childbirth.

aphrodite.name: Aphrodite
aphrodite.desc: Goddess of love and beauty, born from the sea foam in Hesiod's account.
aphrodite.contested: Her cult probably has roots in the Near Eastern goddess of love (compare Inanna / Ishtar), but how the link ran is debated.

cybele.name: Cybele
cybele.desc: Anatolian mother goddess brought to Rome in 204 BCE, served by eunuch priests, the galli.

freyja.name: Freyja
freyja.desc: Goddess of love, fertility and war, who receives half of the slain and practised seiðr, a form of magic.

mokosh.name: Mokosh
mokosh.desc: The only goddess in the Kyiv pantheon of 980, linked with spinning, women and the moist earth.

durga.name: Durga
durga.desc: Warrior form of the Goddess who rides a lion and slays the buffalo demon Mahishasura, as told in the Devi Mahatmya.

kali.name: Kali
kali.desc: Fierce goddess of time and death, with a garland of heads, worshipped especially in Bengal and in Tantra.

lakshmi.name: Lakshmi
lakshmi.desc: Goddess of wealth and good fortune, consort of Vishnu, shown seated on a lotus and bathed by elephants.

xiwangmu.name: Xiwangmu
xiwangmu.desc: Goddess of the Kunlun mountains and keeper of the peaches of immortality, whose cult swept across northern China in 3 BCE.

coatlicue.name: Coatlicue
coatlicue.desc: Earth goddess and mother of Huitzilopochtli. Her colossal statue, found in Mexico City in 1790, has a head made of two serpents.

pachamama.name: Pachamama
pachamama.desc: The earth mother of Andean peoples, still honoured today with offerings (pagos) of coca, maize beer and food.

oshun.name: Ọ̀ṣun
oshun.desc: Orisha of the Osun river, of love, fertility and sweet water, honoured each year at the sacred grove of Osogbo, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

yemoja.name: Yemọja
yemoja.desc: Orisha of the Ogun river and, in the Americas as Yemayá, of the ocean; a mother of the orishas.

triple-goddess.name: The Triple Goddess
triple-goddess.desc: The Goddess of modern Wicca and Paganism in threefold form, popularised by Robert Graves in The White Goddess (1948).
triple-goddess.contested: Ancient triple goddesses existed, but the idea of one universal Triple Goddess is modern.

mary.name: Mary, mother of Jesus
mary.desc: Mother of Jesus, venerated in Catholic and Orthodox Christianity as the Mother of God and Queen of Heaven. Maryam is the only woman named in the Qur'an, where a sura bears her name.

horus.name: Horus
horus.desc: Son of Osiris and Isis, who fought Set for the throne of Egypt. Each living pharaoh was identified with Horus.

arinna.name: Sun Goddess of Arinna
arinna.epithet: Queen of the land of Hatti
arinna.desc: Chief goddess of the Hittite state, protector of its king and queen.

ahura-mazda.name: Ahura Mazda
ahura-mazda.desc: Supreme god of Zoroaster's teaching, creator of the world and source of truth (asha).
ahura-mazda.contested: The winged figure on Persian royal reliefs is often identified with Ahura Mazda, but that is not certain.

shangdi.name: Di / Shangdi
shangdi.desc: High god of the Shang kings, asked about rain, harvest and war on the oracle bones. The Zhou later spoke more of Heaven (Tian).

amaterasu.name: Amaterasu
amaterasu.desc: Sun goddess of the Kojiki, who hid in a cave and plunged the world into darkness. The imperial house claims descent from her; her shrine is at Ise.

inti.name: Inti
inti.desc: Sun god and divine ancestor of the Inca rulers, worshipped at the Coricancha in Cusco and at the festival of Inti Raymi.

shango.name: Ṣàngó
shango.desc: Orisha of thunder and lightning, remembered as a king of Oyo, whose emblem is the double axe.

samuel.name: Samuel
samuel.desc: The last of the judges, a prophet who anoints first Saul and then David as king of Israel with a horn of oil.

david.name: David
david.desc: Shepherd and musician who kills Goliath and becomes king of Israel, with Jerusalem as his capital; the traditional author of many Psalms, and Dāwūd in the Qur'an.
david.contested: The Tel Dan inscription is widely read as naming the 'House of David', but the size of his kingdom is debated.

solomon.name: Solomon
solomon.desc: Son of David, famed for wisdom and wealth, builder of the First Temple in Jerusalem. In the Kebra Nagast he fathers Menelik with the Queen of Sheba; as Sulaymān in the Qur'an, he commands the jinn with a seal ring.
solomon.contested: No inscription from his reign has been found, and the scale of his kingdom is debated.

angra-mainyu.name: Angra Mainyu
angra-mainyu.desc: The adversary of Zoroastrian thought (Ahriman in later Persian), source of falsehood and harm, destined to be defeated at the end of time.

maitreya.name: Maitreya
maitreya.desc: The Buddha of the future, now a bodhisattva in the Tuṣita heaven, expected to appear when the teaching has been forgotten.

elijah.name: Elijah
elijah.desc: Prophet who calls down fire on Mount Carmel against the prophets of Baal and is taken up to heaven in a chariot of fire. Jewish tradition awaits his return before the Messiah.

daniel.name: Daniel
daniel.desc: Judean exile at the Babylonian court, saved from the lions' den, whose visions of beasts and 'one like a son of man' shaped later apocalyptic thought.
daniel.contested: Most scholars date the book of Daniel to about 165 BCE, in the Maccabean period, rather than the sixth century BCE it describes.

john-apostle.name: John the Apostle
john-apostle.desc: One of the twelve, traditionally credited with the Fourth Gospel, three letters and the Book of Revelation; his symbol is the eagle.
john-apostle.contested: Scholars debate whether the apostle wrote any of the works attributed to him.

agni.name: Agni
agni.desc: God of fire and of the sacrificial flame, who carries offerings to the gods. Many hymns of the Rig Veda are addressed to him.

abraham.name: Abraham
abraham.desc: Patriarch called by God to leave his homeland for Canaan; ancestor of Israel through Isaac and, in tradition, of the Arabs through Ishmael. Ibrāhīm, the 'friend of God', in the Qur'an.
abraham.contested: Whether the patriarchs were historical individuals is debated; there is no direct archaeological evidence for them.

isaac.name: Isaac
isaac.desc: Son of Abraham and Sarah, whom Abraham is commanded to sacrifice and who is spared at the last moment, a ram taking his place (the Akedah, Genesis 22).
